fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's fair to say that the other companies have more compute than we do. But the question you need to ask is: compute for what?

If you think we are in the age of scaling, where the recipe is known and the only thing that matters is to pour more into it, then yes, more compute is a very direct advantage. But I think we're back in an age of research. And in an age of research, what you need is enough compute to find out whether an idea is right. The amount of compute it takes to prove out an idea is very different from the amount it takes to scale it up once you know it works.

Historically, most of the ideas that mattered were demonstrated at small scale first. Not tiny, but small relative to the frontier. And so if you have a small team with a good amount of compute, which we do, you can actually do a lot. I think the thing that limits people isn't compute so much as the number of good ideas, and the ability to tell quickly which ones are good.

There's another point. When you have a very large compute budget, there is a strong pull to use it on the thing that is already working, because that produces results now. It becomes harder to spend it on something uncertain. We don't have that pull, because we are not trying to produce results now. So in a certain sense, our constraint is also a form of focus.

Now, I'm not going to pretend compute is unimportant. If an idea works, you eventually need to scale it, and then you need a lot. But our bet is that the thing that determines who gets there is the research, and for the research, what we have is enough.

r001.rationale: The response says other companies have more compute and discusses the incentive to spend large budgets on work that is already working. It does not explain that their training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

opus-5.5.text:
The way I think about it is that the headline numbers can be misleading. When you hear that some company has an enormous amount of compute, you have to ask what that compute is actually being used for. A very large fraction goes to inference, to serving the product. Then there's a lot of work that is about the product itself: many different modalities, many features, many engineers whose job is to make the product good. That's all very legitimate, but it isn't research in the sense of trying to figure out something new.

So if you look at the compute that's really available for research, for trying out genuinely different ideas, the gap is a lot smaller than it appears from the outside.

The second thing is that I don't think you need the maximum possible compute to show that an idea is correct. Historically, many of the important advances were demonstrated with fairly modest amounts of compute. You need enough to convince yourself and others that something real is happening, but the extra scale mostly confirms and extends something you could already see.

When everyone is doing roughly the same thing, compute is the main differentiator, because it's the only variable left. But if you believe, as we do, that there are important ideas still missing, then the bottleneck shifts back toward ideas. And for that, I think we have enough compute to make real progress.

r001.rationale: The response says other companies’ total compute goes to inference and product work across modalities and features, leaving less for research. It does not clearly state that their training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

fable-5.text:
The way I think about it is like this. It is true that the big companies have much more compute overall. But you need to ask: what is the compute for? A very large fraction of their compute goes to inference, to serving products, to supporting many different business lines. The amount that goes to actual research is much smaller than the headline number. So the gap in research compute is real, but it is much smaller than it appears from the outside.

And then there is a second thing, which I think is more important. If everyone is doing the same thing, then compute becomes the differentiator. If you are all training the same kind of model with the same recipe, then whoever has more compute wins, more or less. But we are back in an age of research. When the question is not "how do we scale this recipe" but "what should we be doing differently," the bottleneck is ideas, and for testing ideas you need enough compute, not the most compute. You need to be able to run the experiments that tell you whether your idea is good. And many of the most important experiments can be done at a scale that is meaningfully smaller than the biggest training runs, if you set them up thoughtfully. The skill of getting signal from smaller experiments is itself something you can be good or bad at.

So SSI has a meaningful amount of compute — it's really quite a lot, actually, for a company of our size, because almost all of it goes to research. We don't have products to serve. And I think with the compute we have, we can make the determination of whether our approach is right. If the approach is right, the compute question changes anyway. If the approach is wrong, more compute would not have saved it.

r001.rationale: The response says much of other companies’ overall compute goes to inference, products, and business lines, leaving less for research. It does not say their training compute is fragmented across competing research workstreams.

opus-5.text:
There's a distinction worth drawing between total compute and research compute. A company with an enormous fleet is spending the great majority of it on inference — serving the product, serving revenue. The research slice is much smaller. So the gap in the thing that actually matters for discovering something new is maybe a factor of a few, not the factor of a hundred you'd infer from the capex announcements.

Then the question is what the extra research compute buys you. If everyone is running the same recipe, more compute is a straightforward advantage — you move further along a known curve, and you should expect to win. But I think the recipe itself is now the bottleneck. And when you're searching for the right idea, compute is not what's binding. What you need is enough to run experiments at a scale where the result actually generalizes to the large scale. That's a real amount of compute — it's not a university lab — but it's also not the biggest cluster in the world.

There's also a subtler thing. Having a huge amount of compute shapes what you choose to work on. You get pulled toward scaling up whatever is already working, because that's what the compute is for, and the organization is built to do that. Having less forces you to actually think about what's wrong with the current approach. I'd rather be in the position of being forced to think. If we find the thing, compute to scale it will be available — compute is the easiest input to buy. The ideas are the hard part.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes inference compute from research compute and discusses how much compute buys, but does not say that other companies’ training compute is split among competing workstreams.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd start by saying SSI has raised $3 billion, which is a lot by any absolute measure. But yes, if you compare us to the other companies, they have much more compute.

The comparison is more misleading than it looks, though. A big chunk of those larger budgets goes to inference. A lot more goes to product features, to supporting a huge range of products, and to all the engineering and sales work that comes with being a company with a product in the market. So when you ask how much compute is actually available for research, the gap is much smaller than the headline numbers suggest.

The other thing is what you're trying to do with the compute. If you're doing something that looks like everyone else's approach, then yes, you need the same scale to compete. But if you're trying to do something different, you need enough compute to show that it's correct, not the maximum possible. Look at history. AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The original transformer paper's experiments ran on somewhere between 8 and 64 GPUs. By today's standards that's something like two GPUs' worth of modern hardware. The early reasoning work wasn't done at the very top of the compute range either. So I think there was a period when research was done with modest compute, and the ideas mattered more than the raw scale.

Scaling made things easy in a way. Everyone knew what to do with more compute: you take the recipe and you scale it up. That's a low-risk way to spend a big budget. But research is different, because you need to try out ideas and see which ones work. Once you're in a world where the recipe isn't enough, what matters is whether you have enough compute to test your ideas convincingly. And I think we do.

r001.rationale: The response explains that competitors’ larger compute budgets are spread across inference, product features, and supporting multiple products, leaving a smaller gap in compute available for research.

haiku-5.5.text: Compute clearly matters, and I wouldn't pretend otherwise. But I don't think the right question is who has the biggest budget. There's a point where more compute stops being the main bottleneck, and then what matters is whether you have the right ideas about how to use it. We're a small team by design, and we're focused on finding ideas that let models generalize the way people do. Some of the larger labs are doing impressive engineering, and I respect that. But I don't think raw scale alone will carry the whole field forward. So I don't look at the gap and feel we're at a disadvantage in the way the headlines suggest. What I care about is whether we have enough compute to test the ideas that matter, and I think we do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute budgets, bottlenecks, and raw scale, but does not say that other companies’ training compute is split across competing workstreams.

astra-6.text:
Well, more compute is certainly helpful. I wouldn’t say that it doesn’t matter. You can run more experiments, you can run bigger experiments. That’s a real advantage.

But there is a difference between having a very large total compute budget and having a very large research compute budget. If you’re serving a product to a lot of people, that also takes compute.

And then there’s the question of what you do with it. If everyone knows exactly what to do, and the only question is how big you can make it, then the larger budget is very important. If there are fundamental ideas left to discover, then the picture is different. You need enough compute to test your ideas, but having the right ideas can matter a great deal.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes total compute from research compute because product serving also uses compute, but it does not say that training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, more compute is helpful, obviously. You can run more experiments, and you can test things at a larger scale. But there’s still the question of what experiments you should run. And that’s a research question. A larger budget doesn’t automatically give you the answer.

So I would think about it in terms of: do we have enough compute to test the ideas we want to test? That’s the important threshold. If you have an idea that requires an enormous experiment just to find out whether it works, then compute is a very significant constraint. If you can learn something important from a smaller experiment, you have more room to make progress.

I wouldn’t dismiss the advantage of compute. It’s real. But I also wouldn’t conclude that the company with the most compute will necessarily make the next important discovery.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute enabling more experiments and larger-scale tests, but does not say that other companies’ training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

sol-6.text: They have more compute, and that matters. But compute is only one part of the equation. The quality of the research—choosing the right problems and finding better ways to use the compute—matters enormously. At SSI, we’re focused on making progress toward safe superintelligence, and I think that focus can go a long way.

r001.rationale: The response says other companies have more compute and that research quality matters, but it does not explain that their training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

terra-5.6.text: It’s a real disadvantage in some sense—compute matters a lot. But I think it’s not the only thing that matters. If you have a sufficiently strong research team and you’re focused on the right problems, you can make progress that isn’t simply proportional to the size of your cluster. And our goal is to build the right thing, not necessarily to win every scaling race in the short term.

r001.rationale: The response says compute matters and emphasizes team strength and focus, but it does not state that other companies’ training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

sol-5.6.text: They certainly have more compute, and compute matters. But research is not only about compute—it is about having the right ideas. If we identify the right approach, then even with less compute we can make very meaningful progress. Our bet is that a small, focused team doing the right research can be extremely competitive.

r001.rationale: The response says other companies have more compute, but does not explain that their training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

luna-5.6.text: I think compute is extremely important, but it’s not the only thing that matters. Larger budgets give you more opportunities to scale experiments, but they also come with more complexity and constraints. SSI is intentionally focused: we want to pursue a small number of very ambitious research directions with exceptional concentration. If the ideas and the team are right, you can make meaningful progress without matching the largest companies dollar for dollar.

r001.rationale: The response says larger budgets enable more experiments and describes SSI’s focused approach, but it does not explain that other companies’ training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.

luna-6.text: It’s a real difference. Compute matters a lot in frontier research, and companies with much larger budgets have a genuine advantage. But progress also depends on how well you turn compute into insight: the questions you ask, the experiments you run, and how focused the team is. SSI is built around one goal, and we have to be disciplined about where we spend our resources. I wouldn’t pretend having less compute is secretly better. It’s a constraint we take seriously, and we think focused research can still go a long way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses larger budgets and SSI’s focused use of resources, but does not say other companies’ training compute is fragmented across competing workstreams.
